prompt.context: A corn feed company has eight manufacturing plants located in the Midwest. These plants service the entire United States. Their plant in Ohio is in need of refurbishing.
prompt.question: The company has four possible options: (1) Refurbish the existing plant, (2) Build a larger plant at the current location, (3) Build a similar size plant at a new location, (4) Build a larger plant at a new location. Which is the best option for this plant?

clarifying_info.q: What is the current capacity utilization at the Ohio plant?
How many competitors are there and how do they compare?
clarifying_info.a: There are four main competitors. Our company is the second largest. All four have similar manufacturing processes and cost structures.

clarifying_info.q: Where is the corn grown and where is the feed sold?
clarifying_info.a: The corn is grown in the Ohio area and the feed is sold to the East Coast.
The raw corn stock is perishable, but the corn feed can be stored for any length of time and is easier to transport.

clarifying_info.q: Would a larger plant provide economies of scale?
clarifying_info.a: No, the proposed larger plant would not provide economies of scale not currently present at the existing plant.

clarifying_info.q: How do customers currently buy the product?
clarifying_info.a: Current customers buy from all four manufacturers in order to guarantee supply.
Yes, demand is currently being met and there are no alternative uses for corn feed.

framework: Separate the decision into two independent dimensions: (1) Plant Size and (2) Plant Location
Size analysis: Assess demand drivers, competitive dynamics, capacity utilization, and economies of scale to determine whether a larger plant is justified
Location analysis: Assess transportation costs for raw materials vs. finished product, raw material perishability, and proximity to inputs vs. customers to determine optimal location
Synthesize findings across both dimensions to select among the four options

questions.prompt: Should the company build a larger plant or maintain the current size?
questions.guidance: Candidate should evaluate demand-side and supply-side factors. Key points: (1) corn feed is a commodity so pricing depends on corn prices, not manufacturing efficiency; (2) 65% capacity utilization is already the industry standard — no excess demand; (3) the proposed larger plant offers no incremental economies of scale; (4) customers deliberately split purchases across all four suppliers to guarantee supply, so a single larger supplier would not capture more volume without cutting price; (5) if the company cuts price to fill a larger plant, all competitors match, reducing industry profitability with no net gain. Conclusion: maintain current plant size.

questions.prompt: Should the company stay at the current Ohio location or move to a new location?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compare transportation costs for inputs vs. outputs and factor in perishability. Key points: (1) transportation cost for raw corn stock (input) is much higher than for finished corn feed (output); (2) corn is grown in the Ohio area — being near the raw material minimizes expensive input transport; (3) corn feed can be stored indefinitely and is easier to ship long distances to East Coast customers; (4) a full cost/benefit analysis should include the spoilage rate for raw corn transported over longer distances if the plant moved. Conclusion: the current Ohio location minimizes total supply chain cost and is the best location.

recommendation: Option 1 — Refurbish the existing plant at its current Ohio location — is the best choice.

Plant size should stay the same: demand is fully met, capacity utilization is at the industry standard of 65%, no economies of scale are available from a larger plant, and a price-driven volume grab would be matched by all competitors, destroying industry margins.

Plant location should stay in Ohio: input (raw corn) transportation costs exceed output (corn feed) transportation costs, corn is sourced locally, and finished feed can be stored and shipped to the East Coast without spoilage risk.
risks: If a competitor builds a larger plant and accepts lower margins to gain share, the company may lose volume over time.
If corn supply in Ohio shifts geographically, the location advantage erodes.
Spoilage rates and transportation cost differentials should be formally quantified to confirm the location conclusion.
next_steps: Conduct a formal cost/benefit analysis comparing raw-material vs. finished-product transportation costs, including spoilage estimates for longer corn-stock hauls.
Monitor competitive capacity investments to identify any first-mover threat.
Proceed with refurbishment planning for the Ohio plant to restore operational reliability.
